reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase), the third enzyme of haem biosynthesis, with characteristically low clinical penetrance
Presents with acute neurovisceral attacks: severe poorly localised abdominal pain without peritonism, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension and hyponatraemia
Neuropsychiatric features include peripheral (predominantly motor) neuropathy, seizures, agitation, confusion and, in severe cases, respiratory muscle weakness
This is an acute porphyria without photocutaneous involvement, since the accumulating substances are the non-photosensitising precursors rather than photoreactive porphyrins
The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised urinary aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) during an attack, with PBG typically elevated more than in the hepatic coproporphyrias
Attacks are precipitated by porphyrinogenic drugs, fasting or reduced calorie intake, alcohol, infection, and hormonal fluctuations such as the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle

Management centres on removing triggers, high carbohydrate/glucose loading for mild attacks and intravenous haem for severe or progressive attacks, alongside supportive care and pain control with safe analgesics
Hyponatraemia during attacks is common and may reflect SIADH or gastrointestinal losses and requires careful correction
reference.pathophysiology: Acute intermittent porphyria results from partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase, the third enzyme of the haem biosynthetic pathway, which condenses porphobilinogen molecules. When hepatic haem demand rises, the rate-limiting enzyme ALA synthase is induced; the downstream bottleneck causes accumulation of the early precursors ALA and PBG. These precursors, particularly ALA, are thought to be neurotoxic and underlie the neurovisceral manifestations. Because no photoreactive porphyrins accumulate, the skin is spared. Enzyme activity is typically around half of normal, so most carriers remain asymptomatic unless exposed to precipitating factors that upregulate hepatic haem synthesis.
additionalDifferentials: Surgical acute abdomen (appendicitis, bowel obstruction, perforation)
Lead poisoning, which also raises ALA and causes neuropathy
Guillain-Barre syndrome and other acute peripheral neuropathies
Hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria (other acute porphyrias)
Functional or psychiatric abdominal pain syndromes
Hyponatraemia of other cause with confusion or seizures
additionalInvestigations: Spot (fresh, light-protected) urinary porphobilinogen and ALA, ideally taken during symptoms
Quantitative urinary, faecal and plasma porphyrin profiling to distinguish from other acute porphyrias
Molecular genetic testing of the HMBS gene to confirm diagnosis and enable family screening
Serum sodium and renal function to detect and monitor hyponatraemia
Nerve conduction studies where motor neuropathy is suspected
redFlags: Progressive motor weakness or bulbar/respiratory involvement threatening ventilatory failure
Seizures, especially when compounded by hyponatraemia
Severe autonomic instability with dangerous hypertension or arrhythmia
Recurrent unexplained severe abdominal pain in a young adult, especially a woman, with a family history
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition, trigger avoidance and treatment most attacks resolve, though recovery from severe neuropathy can be slow and incomplete. Recurrent attacks, chronic pain, and long-term risks including hypertension, renal impairment and hepatocellular carcinoma may complicate the course.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent abdominal pain to a functional or psychiatric cause and missing the diagnosis
Administering porphyrinogenic drugs (many anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, and others) that precipitate or worsen attacks
Failing to collect and protect urine promptly, so a raised PBG level is missed
Overlooking that low penetrance means most gene carriers never have symptoms, complicating family counselling
Aggressive fasting for investigations or surgery without carbohydrate cover
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Intravenous haem arginate to suppress ALA synthase and abort the acute attack
Carbohydrate loading with glucose for mild attacks and as adjunct during treatment
Immediate withdrawal of porphyrinogenic drugs and correction of precipitants such as fasting, alcohol, and infection
Symptom control with opioid analgesia, antiemetics, beta-blockers for tachycardia and hypertension, and safe anticonvulsants such as levetiracetam or gabapentin for seizures
Monitor and correct hyponatraemia and observe for respiratory muscle weakness requiring ventilatory support
Prophylaxis of recurrent attacks with givosiran or gonadotrophin-releasing hormone analogues for cyclical menstrual attacks
Genetic counselling with HMBS testing of relatives and a lifelong personalised list of safe and unsafe drugs
Referral to a specialist porphyria centre
